title: Where do you draw the fail-closed line?
summary:
Every release pipeline has checks that can stop the line. The interesting question is what a check does when it can't finish its own job — when coverage is partial, a source times out, or half the inputs are missing.

Fail open, and the release goes out with a quiet gap in it. Fail closed, and the release stops on what might be a tooling hiccup. Both choices have a cost; the mistake is not knowing which one each of your checks makes.

Our release gate withholds its score when coverage is partial. Not a low score — no score at all, a literal "WITHHELD", because a number computed from half the evidence is worse than none: it looks like knowledge and gets quoted like knowledge. We landed there after watching the alternative in the wild — a scoring tool that printed confident grades on runs it had only partly observed, and people downstream made decisions on them.

title: One API Key, Many Routes: Calling AI Video Models in Python with Automatic Failover
summary:
A single API key should not lock you into a single upstream. When you generate AI video at scale, the model you pick today can be rate-limited, throttled, or temporarily down tomorrow. The fix is a multi-route setup: one gateway key, many video models behind it, and automatic failover when a route fails.

Here is the idea in Python:

  1. Call the models endpoint to list available video routes.
  2. Pick a model code and submit a generation task with an idempotency key.
  3. Poll the task until it reaches a terminal state (success / failed / expired).
  4. If a route fails, retry the next route in order — automatically.

Why it matters:

  • Reliability: a failed upstream does not fail your user request.
  • Cost control: different routes have different prices; pick per tier.
  • No vendor lock-in: swap models by changing one code string.

One pnpm workspace, five Workers, one shared package. Each Worker is its own product with its own name, key, quota and failure domain. A bug in the PDF parser cannot take down email verification.

title: KVM's AMD Nested-Reset Bug Changes the Boundary Between Tenants
summary:
KVM's AMD Nested-Reset Bug Changes the Boundary Between Tenants

A virtual machine is supposed to contain an untrusted workload. KVM's boundary is the promise that the guest cannot reach the host kernel, another tenant's memory, or the hardware state that ties them together. CVE-2026-99312 breaks that promise on a specific AMD configuration: a Linux KVM host with nested virtualization enabled, running an affected kernel, and hosting a guest whose owner has root inside the VM.

The flaw is a use-after-free in KVM's nested SVM page-table handling. When a virtual CPU receives an INIT while an L2 guest is running with paging disabled, KVM can return to the outer VM without resetting memory-management state. The outer VM retains a pointer to a nested page table that has already been freed. If the host later reuses that page, the guest can populate it with entries that cause the processor to follow mappings into host physical memory.
